title: What makes the UI/UX of a management game genuinely great?
author: Sea-Word130
selftext:
I’m making an airline management game with detailed scheduling, fleet operations and cabin design. The systems are playable, but I’m struggling with how to present all that depth clearly.

For people who play management games: which games make complex decisions feel easy to navigate? What do they do well with information density, repeated tasks and finding the right screen quickly? And which UI choices frustrate you, even in games you otherwise love?

Specific games or screenshots would be especially helpful. I’m trying to figure out what to prioritize as I redesign the interface.

comments.author: Revolutionary-Skin97
comments.body:
For me, the screen should always ensure the following is delivered to the player:

From top left to top right:
 the player should be able to decide what he can do next and what to prepare for.

From bottom left to bottom right:
The player should be able to go to places where he can get more information on how to plan more.

Center screen:
All execution should be held here, whether its consumption of resources, setting up, etc.

replies.author: Sea-Word130
replies.body: So on an information-dense screen, what would you most want to keep visible at all times?

replies.author: Revolutionary-Skin97
replies.body:
Resource list

A button to go to where can I use them

A screen panel to consume them to give me dopamine.

replies.author: Sea-Word130
replies.body: Got it, thanks! I’ll try to incorporate this into my game！

comments.author: Sea-Word130
comments.body: Got it, thanks! I’ll try to incorporate this into my game！

comments.author: klas-klattermus
comments.body: Decisions should be interesting, at a certain scale I want my micro to be managed for me and only be distributed if something interesting actually happens

replies.author: Sea-Word130
replies.body: That’s a good point. So as the airline grows, you’d rather have routine operations become increasingly automated, with the UI mainly surfacing exceptions and decisions that actually need your attention?

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Yeah, and that attention should not be "shift those crates blocking the baggage claim" or anything else that a worker could do. If anything it should be policy decisions like A "from now on all workers in [region] needs to have [certificate] , this will prevent this from happening again but reduce the hiring pool and increase base salary by [x]" or B "whenever this happens, give travelers a [y] refund" so I can plan for if I want to remove the problem at a long term  average cost or keep the problem at a lower but spiking cost, or C ignore the problem and let it solve itself but bad publicity reduces travelers on the affected line for some weeks every time it happens.

replies.author: Sea-Word130
replies.body:
I really like that idea — especially turning recurring operational problems into policy decisions rather than making the player solve the same event repeatedly. That would also make scaling an airline feel more like actually managing an organization rather than just doing more micromanagement.  
Thanks a lot！

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
From a technical perspective, once you reach a certain point you can just hide and replace the old mechanic.
If level 1 was a blinking UI element informing you that the baggage escalator needed manual unblocking then at level 2 you can either fix it yourself, reassign a worker or hire an extra permanent or temp worker (fixed cost) to fix it. The real problem now is to solve why that thing happens, but you can temporarily solve it by sacrificing your time instead of money because at this scale it might matter. On level 3 however, this becomes a policy problem rather than something you have time to handle manually, so your choice is now how to handle that bigger decision. And you will no longer even see or access the blocked room, it's beneath your paygrade

replies.author: Sea-Word130
replies.body: I really like the idea of the abstraction level changing as the airline grows. Instead of just giving the player more and more things to manage, the game could actually remove lower-level interactions and replace them with higher-level decisions. That would make growth feel meaningful beyond just having more aircraft and money.

comments.author: 12redandblack12
comments.body:
other people have made good suggestions, a couple of things from an accessibility point of view: colorblind mode is nice, eg. shifting reds to blues [you can google colorblind-friendly palettes]; preferably customizable, and stronger outlines. 

i also don't like being flooded with text and icons: what is relevant to the part of the game i'm playing should be displayed [i don't need my hp bar at all times in a story-heavy rpg for example], extraneous information in different menus that are easy to access with as few clicks as possible to reach. if your game has a codex/wiki or something like that [eg the civilopedia in the civ games], hyperlinks are good to reach other pages.

comments.author: bigorangemachine
comments.body:
I think its better to take an incremental approach. Like Civ5 you have the depth available the whole time but as you scale the difficulty you need to set your cities off auto and tweak then yourself.

I think now a days a search with auto suggest is best.

comments.author: GamesByAI
comments.body:
For your airline game, I'd organize the interface around decisions: assign an aircraft, fix a scheduling conflict, then check what that change costs. Fleet operations, scheduling and cabin design can remain separate systems without making the player carry information between three screens.

Try a flight detail panel that keeps the selected aircraft, route, timetable and relevant constraints visible together. Preview the consequences before confirming a change. For repeated work, let players copy a schedule and edit the exceptions.

A useful redesign test: give someone an aircraft with a scheduling conflict and ask them to resolve it without help. Note every screen change and every number they have to remember. That should give you a concrete priority list.
